messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 80
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Data Scientist
  trauma_type: Relief worker in war zone
  pcl5: 50

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Moral Violation: People misbehaving, Entrapment: Having no options, Dream Residue: Waking up from a nightmare
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid News: News reports about events similar to what happened to me, Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Memory: Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
  Negative Appraisals: Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy, Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

At 80, Minh Tran still speaks about the war-zone deployment as if parts of it are unfolding in the next room. Years earlier, as a relief worker coordinating food and medical distribution in a besieged city, he had spent days negotiating with armed men at makeshift checkpoints while families waited behind him. The moment that stays with him most sharply came when a truck of supplies was blocked and civilians were shoved back from the road. He remembers the chaos of people pleading, the humiliation and cruelty of men misusing power, and the sickening conviction that there were no good options left to him. If he argued, he risked provoking violence; if he complied, he felt he was participating in something unforgivable. That scene now seems to organize much of what still troubles him: people behaving badly, any situation in which he feels cornered, and the disorienting minutes after waking from a nightmare all strike him with a force that feels out of proportion to the present but entirely faithful to what happened there.

In the years since returning to the United States, Minh has continued working as a data scientist, mostly remotely after his wife died. Even in ordinary professional settings, the old meanings flood back. In video meetings, if a colleague talks over someone junior or behaves selfishly, Minh feels a jolt of moral alarm. If a project discussion narrows and he feels boxed into a decision, he becomes tense and fixed on escape routes, as though once again there are no acceptable choices. On mornings when he wakes from a nightmare, the residue of it clings to him so strongly that the day begins under threat. In those moments he is certain the world is dangerous, and what frightens him most is how quickly anger rises in him; he has come to believe these reactions may mean he is going crazy, or that he could lose control of his rage and do something terrible.

Those triggers do not stay as thoughts for long. When a client call is scheduled, he rehearses every possible exchange beforehand, trying to prevent being trapped or provoked. If he has slept badly after a nightmare, he avoids news coverage altogether, especially reports about sieges, displaced civilians, or aid failures, because even a headline can pull him back. He also scans constantly: in the grocery store, in the lobby of his apartment building, even while sitting at his computer, his eyes move to doors, faces, sudden noises. What began as a way to stay safe has gradually narrowed his days. He turns down collaborative meetings when he can, keeps conversations brief, and structures his work around control and predictability.

The memories themselves are not experienced as recollections. Minh describes them as a film that starts playing without his consent, with the same road, the same pleading voices, the same split-second calculations. When it comes, he is not remembering from a distance; he feels it happening right now. A raised voice in a meeting, the sight of petty cruelty in public, or that trapped feeling when options seem to close can bring the whole sequence forward with such immediacy that his body goes rigid and ready. After nights broken by nightmares, this happens even more easily, and he moves through the morning as if the city around him were only a thin layer over the checkpoint road.

These episodes feed the meanings he has made of himself and the world. Each time the memory arrives so vividly, Minh takes it as evidence that something in his mind is breaking down. When he notices how angry he feels at other people’s selfishness or bullying, he does not experience that as understandable outrage but as proof that he may someday erupt. Because he sees the world as fundamentally dangerous, he watches more closely for signs of moral violation or entrapment, and this makes those very moments stand out everywhere to him: in news clips he tries not to watch, in overheard conversations, in routine workplace disagreements. The more he anticipates them, the more quickly they seem to find him.

His efforts to manage this have also deepened the problem. Rehearsing conversations leaves him entering interactions already keyed up, listening for the line that will corner or provoke him. Constantly checking his surroundings means he is repeatedly noticing the very cues that set him off. Avoiding the news gives temporary relief, but when something slips through—an image on a homepage, a radio report in a rideshare—it hits with full force, and the old film runs again. He has become increasingly irritable, snapping at coworkers in ways that shame him afterward, then withdrawing further because that feels like proof his anger is dangerous.

Minh finally sought help after abruptly ending a long call with a junior analyst who had simply challenged one of his assumptions. For several minutes afterward he stood in his kitchen trembling, heart pounding, convinced he had nearly become the man he feared. He is asking for treatment now because he is exhausted by living in a body that feels constantly braced for danger, and because he wants to believe that these reactions do not mean he is losing his mind. More than anything, he hopes he can learn to wake from a nightmare and know, fully, that he is here and not there.
